The Least storm petrel (Oceanodroma microsoma) is one of the smallest seabirds in the Californian current system, and its life history reflects a tight energetic budget. At typical active body temperatures of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], the maximum rate of annual reproductive output is approximately one egg per year [Ri = approximately one egg per year], a remarkably low fecundity that is consistent with its pelagic foraging ecology and the high energetic cost of a single prolonged breeding attempt. Incubation of the single-egg clutch occurs in deep rock crevices or rodent burrows, where the thermal environment is buffered from ambient fluctuations; the incubation period for a closely related congener, Oceanodroma leucorhoa, proceeds at approximately 36 °C [T = 36 °C] and lasts about 41 days [ab = about 41 days], and comparable values are assumed for the least storm petrel. The resulting hatchling, weighing just 4.0 grams [Wwb = 4.0 grams], is altricial and entirely dependent on parental provisioning.

Nestlings exhibit a rapid phase of mass gain, although they never attain large body sizes compared to other procellariiforms. The ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult is roughly 30 grams [Wwi = roughly 30 grams], a figure that places this species among the lightest in its genus. This modest adult body mass imposes a correspondingly low daily maintenance requirement, yet the energetic demands of chick rearing remain substantial relative to the bird's size. Under the thermal conditions of a cool-temperate marine environment (39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]), fledging occurs approximately 88 days after birth [tx = approximately 88 days after birth], a notably long nestling period for such a small bird that reflects the constrained feeding rates of a species reliant on patchily distributed zooplankton. The fledgling then completes its development at sea, achieving nutritional independence only gradually.

The long developmental trajectory continues through the juvenile stage, with puberty, defined as the onset of gonadal maturation, estimated at 264 days after birth [tp = 264 days after birth] under the typical body temperature regimen of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. This delayed attainment of sexual maturity is a common pattern among Procellariiformes, where the building of sufficient body condition for the energetic demands of reproduction requires an extended pre-breeding period. During this phase, subadult birds refine their foraging skills over vast oceanic distances, gradually accumulating the fat reserves necessary to sustain the prolonged incubation and chick-feeding shifts characteristic of the family. Field records suggest that first-year birds engage in prospecting behaviors and may visit colonies prior to actual breeding, but they do not initiate a nesting attempt until nearly a full year has elapsed since their own fledging.

Age at first reproduction represents a further postponement beyond the point of simple gonadal maturity. The time since birth at first brood has been documented at approximately 5 years [tR = approximately 5 years] for Oceanodroma leucorhoa, and comparable demographic patterns inferred for Oceanodroma microsoma suggest a similar first brood age of approximately 5 years [tR = approximately 5 years] when maintained at an active body temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. This extremely late first reproduction is among the most extreme delays documented for any bird of this size class and is hypothesized to reflect the severe constraints on energy acquisition in an oligotrophic foraging environment. The single-egg clutch [N_R_i = single-egg clutch] is laid annually [F_R_i = is laid annually], which underscores that a lifetime reproductive output is accumulated over many years rather than through high per-season fecundity. Individuals that survive the high early mortality associated with nesting on exposed islands may breed repeatedly over a long adult tenure.

Maximum lifespan in this species has been estimated at 36 years [am = 36 years] under the thermal conditions of the active metabolic state (39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]), a value derived from mark-recapture studies in related storm petrel species. Such longevity is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes high adult survival over annual reproductive effort, a pattern widely observed among seabirds that forage in resource-poor oceanic regions. Over the course of a 5-year delay from birth to first brood (5 years from birth to first brood) [tR = 5 years from birth to first brood], a bird that survives to adulthood still has decades ahead of it to contribute to the population at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. This extreme delay, combined with a single-egg clutch produced annually, defines a life-history pace that is among the slowest recorded for any avian species globally, reflecting the severe constraints of a pelagic existence on a tiny body frame.
